379.title: Four kinds of happiness
379.hook: having wealth, using it well, owing no debt, and being blameless (AN 4.62)
379.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use this sutta to show that householders may rightly enjoy honestly earned wealth, while counting a clear conscience as the greatest happiness; Anathapindika is remembered in the tradition as the model generous lay follower.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five trades, the goods a lay follower doesn't deal in, and a question to keep: what your money does.

A merchant covers a whole park in gold coins, by the old story, to buy it for the Buddha's community. His name is Anathapindika, of the city of Savatthi, and it means feeder of the unprotected, for all the food he gave away. So when the Buddha talks to him about money, he isn't lecturing someone on thrift. He's talking to a man with more than enough. And he names four kinds of happiness that wealth can touch, and says one of them outweighs the other three put together.
screen: `A PARK PAVED IN GOLD.` → `FEEDER OF THE UNPROTECTED.` → `ONE OUTWEIGHS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The first is the happiness of having: wealth earned, the sutta says, by hard work, by the strength of your arms and the sweat of your brow, rightly gained. It counts as a real happiness. The Buddha doesn't tell a householder that money is shameful. The second is the happiness of using it: enjoying your wealth and doing good with it, for yourself, your family, your friends and worthy causes. Money sitting untouched is only half a pleasure. The third is owing nothing, no debt, large or small. A credit card bill that keeps growing shows what it's like when this one is missing. The fourth is blamelessness: knowing that what you've done with body, speech and mind carries no fault. Then the closing verse. The first three, the Buddha says, aren't worth a sixteenth part of the fourth, an old Indian idiom for a tiny fraction. It isn't a choice between them; a householder can have all four. The sutta simply ranks them. You can be wealthy, generous and debt-free, and still uneasy if you know how the money was made. And you can have very little, owe nothing, and sleep like a stone, because there's nothing in your day you need to hide.
screen: `THE HAPPINESS OF HAVING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF USING.` · `THE HAPPINESS OF OWING NOTHING.` · `BLAMELESSNESS OUTWEIGHS THEM ALL.` · then, large: `BLAMELESS IS BEST.`

segments.voice: Go through the four slowly and look for a trace of each in your own life: something you have, however small; something you used well or shared; a debt paid off, or never taken on; something you did this week that you don't need to hide. Rest longest on whichever one you find, and let it be a real happiness, the way the sutta says it is.
Anavajja-sukha, the happiness of blamelessness. Having, using, owing nothing, and blamelessness; the Buddha tells Anathapindika the last outweighs the rest.
Your line: blameless is best. Wealth is a real happiness, and a clear conscience is a bigger one. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

380.title: Four parts
380.hook: to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, one kept for hard times (DN 31)
380.carry: enjoy some, build with some, protect some
380.howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is widely taught to lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, as practical guidance for family, friendship, work and money.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anavajja-sukha, the happiness of blamelessness, which outweighs having, using and owing nothing. Blameless is best.

Early morning near Rajagaha. A young man named Sigala stands with his clothes and hair still wet, bowing in six directions: east, south, west, north, down and up. His dying father told him to, and he does it faithfully, without knowing why. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Then, gently, he reinterprets the whole ritual: the six directions are the people in your life. What follows is a whole sutta of advice for ordinary life, and somewhere in the middle of it, there's a budget.
screen: `WET HAIR, SIX BOWS.` → `HIS FATHER'S LAST WISH.` → `THE BUDDHA STOPS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: East is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your spouse and children. North, your friends. Below, those who work for you. Above, spiritual teachers. For each, the Buddha lists what you owe them and what they owe you. Then, in a run of verses, he turns to money. The wise person gathers wealth the way a bee gathers nectar, a little at a time, and it grows the way an anthill grows. Then the budget: divide your wealth into four parts. Live on one part and enjoy it. Put two parts to work in your business. Keep the fourth saved against hard times. It would still make sense on a spreadsheet. Notice what it assumes: a householder will have money, should enjoy some, should invest in their livelihood, and should plan for misfortune. Nothing here is otherworldly. The fractions don't map neatly onto a modern paycheck, and the tradition doesn't treat them as law; some read the two parts for work as money invested, others as the costs of running a trade. The shape is the lesson: enjoy some, build with some, protect some, and decide on purpose. The commentary, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa, calls this sutta the discipline of the householder. Monks have their rules. This is a lay person's.

segments.voice: Without opening any app, picture your money in four piles, roughly as it is right now: the part you live on, the part that builds your work and your future, the part kept for hard times. Don't calculate; just notice the shape, how it feels in the body to look at it, and whether one small adjustment suggests itself.

Your line: enjoy some, build with some, protect some. One for living, two for work, one for the rainy day. See you tomorrow.

381.title: Work as practice
381.hook: a Chan saying tied to Baizhang: a day without work, a day without food
381.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, daily work periods are part of the schedule, and residents and retreatants clean, cook and garden in silence as practice; in Japanese temples this is called samu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four parts. One to live on, two for work, one for hard times: enjoy some, build with some, protect some.
screen: `FOUR PARTS — ENJOY SOME, BUILD WITH SOME, PROTECT SOME.`

segments.voice: An old Chan master, well past the age for field work, still goes out each day to work the monastery fields with the younger monks. They worry about him, so one day they hide his tools. He doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask him why, he answers, so the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. The master is Baizhang, of Tang-dynasty China, and the line has carried his name ever since.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE FIELDS.` → `THE TOOLS GO MISSING.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: In India, by the old monastic rules, monks didn't farm or dig the soil. They walked for alms and lived on what the village gave. When the teaching traveled to China, things changed. Some monasteries stood in remote mountains, far from any village to feed them, and Chan communities began to farm, cook, haul water and chop wood for themselves. Tradition credits Baizhang with the first rules for Chan monasteries, built around shared labor. The original text is lost, and some historians think much of the story was told later, but the ideal stuck. Work wasn't a break from practice. It was practice. In Japan the same idea is called samu: work done as meditation, sweeping, weeding, scrubbing, in silence and fully. That connects quietly to right livelihood. Few jobs let you choose every task, but you can choose how you're present for it. Sweeping a floor with your whole attention and sweeping it while rehearsing an argument are two different afternoons, even if the floor ends up equally clean. The saying is sometimes taken as a hard rule: no work, no lunch. The story suggests something gentler. Baizhang isn't punishing anyone, not even himself. For him, working and eating simply belonged together, the way breathing in and breathing out do.
screen: `IN INDIA, MONKS DIDN'T FARM.` · `CHAN MONASTERIES PICK UP HOES.` · `SAMU: WORK AS MEDITATION.` · `TWO AFTERNOONS, ONE CLEAN FLOOR.` · then, large: `WORK IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Choose one task you'll do today anyway, the dishes, an email, folding laundry, and picture doing it the Chan way: not faster, not slower, fully, your hands on this plate, this towel. When the mind runs ahead to the next task, come back to this one, and stay with it here for a while, with the breath.
Baizhang. His saying, a day without work is a day without food: in Chan, ordinary labor is part of the path.
Your line: work is practice. The floor ends up just as clean; the afternoon is different. That's day three hundred eighty-one.

382.title: Enough
382.hook: contentment is the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204); greed makes any amount too little
382.howItsDone: Buddhist texts praise contentment often; monastics practice it by living with a few requisites, and lay Buddhists often reflect on it when they recite or study the Dhammapada and the Mangala Sutta, which lists contentment among the highest blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baizhang, still working the fields in old age. Work is practice, done with your whole attention.

There was once a king, the old stories say, who could make it rain money. He'd clap his hands, and gold coins would fall from the sky until they were knee-deep. He ruled the whole earth. Then he wanted heaven, and got it: first the heaven of the four great kings, then the higher heaven where Sakka, king of the gods, gave him half his throne. And sitting on half a throne in paradise, King Mandhatu had one small thought: why only half?
screen: `A KING WHO MAKES IT RAIN GOLD.` → `HALF A THRONE IN HEAVEN.` → `WHY ONLY HALF?`

segments.voice: The moment he thought it, the story says, his power drained away. He fell back to earth, into his own garden, an old man, and died there. The tradition tells this story alongside a short verse of the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's translation: "There is no satisfying lusts, even by a shower of gold pieces." That's Mandhatu's rain. He didn't want something wicked. Wanting simply has no built-in stopping point: whatever you have, greed can make it feel too little. A raise feels like enough for a while, then the new number becomes the floor. Another verse, which you may remember from the first year, gives the alternative in four words. Müller has it: "contentedness the best riches." The Pali is santuṭṭhi: contentment, being satisfied with what's here. It's called riches, not poverty. Contentment isn't settling for less, and it isn't a ban on ever wanting anything. In this tradition it's a wealth you can actually keep, because it doesn't depend on the number. That closes six days on livelihood. Earn clean. Watch what your money does. Count blamelessness above it all. Divide it wisely. Work with your whole attention. And at some point, say the one word greed can't say: enough.

segments.voice: Picture your home and pick one thing, a coat, your bed, the food in your kitchen, and say quietly: this is enough. If something inside argues, let it talk and stay with the thing anyway, then try the breath itself: this breath is enough.
Enough. Santuṭṭhi, contentment: the Dhammapada calls it the best riches, because greed can make any amount feel too little.
Your line: contentment is the best riches. It's a wealth that doesn't depend on the number. Till tomorrow.

383.title: Right effort
383.hook: four efforts: to prevent, to abandon, to arouse, to maintain (AN 4.13)
383.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often present right effort through the four right strivings, and practitioners use them to decide what a moment of practice needs: restraint, letting go, cultivating, or sustaining.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enough. The Dhammapada calls contentment the best riches, a wealth that doesn't depend on the number.

Anyone who has kept a garden knows there are four jobs. Keep weed seeds from blowing in. Pull the weeds that have already come up. Plant what you want to grow. And water what's already growing, so it doesn't wilt. Skip any one, and the garden suffers, however hard you work at the other three. The Buddha gave the sixth factor of his path the same four-part shape: two jobs about the harmful, two about the good.
screen: `KEEP THE SEEDS OUT.` → `PULL WHAT CAME UP.` → `PLANT, AND WATER.`

segments.voice: Sammā vāyāma. Vāyāma means effort, exertion, striving. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha lays out four right strivings. For unwholesome states that haven't arisen: work so they don't arise. For unwholesome states that have arisen: work to let them go. For wholesome states that haven't arisen: work to bring them about. For wholesome states that have arisen: work to keep them from fading, and help them grow to fullness. The next sutta gives them short names: restraint, abandoning, developing, protecting. Each uses the same string of verbs: you generate desire, make an effort, rouse energy, apply your mind, and strive. Desire is in there on purpose; the wish to do good is part of the engine. Two things about the shape. It's balanced: half of right effort is about growing and keeping the good, and people new to practice often pour everything into the first two and forget the gardener's last two jobs. And each asks for a different kind of effort. Preventing is quiet, like latching a gate. Abandoning is active, like pulling a weed. Arousing takes initiative, like planting. Maintaining takes patience, like daily watering. So the question isn't only am I trying hard enough. It's which of the four this moment needs. The next four days take them one at a time.

segments.voice: Let your mind walk the last day like a gardener walking the rows: something unhelpful you can see coming, something already sprouting that needs pulling, something good to plant, something good already growing that needs water. Don't fix anything; choose one of the four, and let your attention rest there with the breath.
Sammā vāyāma. Right effort: prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain. The sixth factor of the path.
Your line: four efforts. Prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain: two for the harmful, two for the good. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.

384.title: Preventing
384.hook: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't arise
384.howItsDone: Monastics practice sense restraint by keeping their gaze lowered on the alms round and avoiding entertainment; lay Buddhists often apply it on observance days and, today, to how they use screens and media.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vayama, right effort, in four jobs: prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain.

Someone opens their phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later they're watching a stranger renovate a bathroom in another country, vaguely annoyed, and a little less fond of their own bathroom. Nobody decided any of that. It came in through the eyes, one tap at a time. Nobody broke down the door. It was simply left open. Today, the first of the four efforts: the one that works before anything goes wrong.
screen: `JUST CHECKING THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `THE DOOR WAS LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is saṃvara, restraint, and the suttas give it a specific picture: guarding the doors of the senses. Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: six doors. In the standard passage, when a practitioner sees a form with the eye, they don't grab at its signs and features, the details that set wanting or irritation going. Left unguarded, that door would let greedy and painful states pour in. So they guard the eye, the ear, and every other door. Notice what this doesn't say. It doesn't say shut your eyes, or never look at anything lovely. Seeing is fine. The guarding happens one step later, at the grab: the moment the mind zooms in, replays, wants more, or wants it gone. That's where the gatekeeper stands. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's words: "Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear", and the verse runs on through every door. It's a quiet effort, and easy to overlook. Abandoning a mood once it's raging is hard work. Not letting it in costs very little, like fixing a slow leak instead of bailing out a flooded basement. And the doors now include a glowing rectangle, often built to keep the eyes on it.

segments.voice: With your eyes open and your gaze resting low, let things come into view without following them: a color, a shape, a sound from outside. Each time the mind starts to grab, to zoom in, judge or spin a story, let the thing simply be seen or heard; nothing has to be shut out, and nothing has to be chased.
Preventing. Saṃvara, restraint: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't get in. The first of the four efforts.
Your line: guard the gate. The guard stands at the grab, not the glance. See you tomorrow.

385.title: Abandoning
385.hook: five ways with a bad thought: replace it, see its danger, ignore it, calm its cause, and at last suppress it (MN 20)
385.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools teach these five methods for working with persistent thoughts, often recommending the gentler ones first and keeping forceful suppression for emergencies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: preventing. Guard the gate at the grab, not the glance, and less gets in.

Some thoughts get past the gate anyway. You're lying in bed and the argument from lunch starts replaying. Or a craving that won't quit. Or a worry, looping like a song you can't stand. Just let it go is easy advice to give. It rarely comes with instructions. The Buddha gave some: five ways, in order, from gentlest to strongest, each with its own picture. The first one is a carpenter's trick.
screen: `THE ARGUMENT REPLAYS.` → `JUST LET IT GO.` → `BUT HOW?`

segments.voice: The sutta, in the Middle Length Discourses, is named for the stilling of thoughts. Way one: when an unwholesome thought keeps coming, turn the mind to another sign, one connected with the wholesome. If it's anger, kindness. If it's craving, something that cools it. Like a skilled carpenter, the Buddha says, who knocks out a coarse peg with a finer one: you drive a better peg in, and it pushes the old one through. Way two: look at the danger in the thought. Where is this taking me? He compares it to a young person fond of finery, horrified to find a carcass hung around their neck. Way three: simply don't attend to it, like someone who closes their eyes or looks away. Way four: calm the thought's momentum, like a man walking fast who asks, why am I hurrying? He slows down, then stands, then sits, then lies down. Way five, the last resort: teeth clenched, tongue pressed to the roof of the mouth, hold the mind down with the mind, like a strong man pinning a weaker one. The order is the lesson. Force comes last, not first. It's tempting to start at way five, and that's the one that wears a person out. Look back at the week: blameless is best, four parts, work is practice, enough, four efforts, guard the gate, and today, a finer peg.
screen: `A FINER PEG FOR A COARSE ONE.` · `SEE THE DANGER.` · `LOOK AWAY, THEN SLOW DOWN.` · `FORCE COMES LAST.` · then, large: `A FINER PEG.`

segments.voice: Let a small, sticky thought come up, nothing overwhelming, and notice what kind it is: irritation, craving, worry. Then choose its finer peg, that person on a good day, the cool, complete breath, one thing that's fine right now, and gently drive it in, letting it push the old one through.
Abandoning. The second effort: letting go of unwholesome thoughts already here. The sutta gives five ways, gentlest first.
Your line: a finer peg. Force comes last, never first. Three hundred eighty-five days, and a week done.
